problem: Prior neural (NeRF/Gaussian-splatting) simulators for robot RL are proprietary or unavailable, poorly documented and irreproducible; conventional 3D simulators need manual modelling and suffer a visual sim-to-real gap.
motivation: Embodied-AI policies trained end-to-end from vision depend on simulator realism, but hand-built environments are costly and diverge visually from the real world. Photorealistic simulators built from a single video could remove this cost, yet no open tooling exists for building them.
key_idea: SplatGym builds an open-source Gymnasium RL environment from a single video, using Gaussian Splatting (nerfstudio splatfacto) for real-time ego-view rendering and an OctoMap octree with FCL for fast collision detection.
insight: Gaussian splatting gives 7.8 ms/frame inference versus 2270 ms for nerfacto (291x faster) with comparable quality, which makes RL sample-hungry training practical. Curriculum learning speeds convergence (the no-curriculum curve converges much more slowly), and pose-noise regularization improves real-world action agreement from 0.612 to 0.783, which supports the sim-to-real claim. This evidence is small-scale: a single garden scene, and the real-world test is offline action matching against human labels.
method: Novel view synthesis: nerfstudio splatfacto Gaussian Splatting trained from COLMAP-posed frames of a hand-held phone video (about 20 min on a 2070 Super) and rendered at arbitrary 6DoF poses.
Point cloud extraction: a NeRF model is also trained (nerfstudio can only export point clouds from NeRF), then cropped manually by x/y/z limits to remove noise.

Octree collision map: the cropped cloud is voxelised coarsely, each voxel becomes an 8-level OctoMap octree (75 octrees, 287,069 points reduced to 10,196 occupied voxels), queried with FCL in under 5 µs per tree; pybind11 exposes it to Python.
Gymnasium environment: 64x64 RGB ego observation, 6 discrete actions (fixed x/y steps, z rotation), sparse reward (+50 goal, -0.2 per step, -10 collision, -10 out of bounds), 200-step cap.
Automatic curriculum: start positions begin near the goal and move outward as the agent succeeds, then become random.
Virtual object overlay: a 3D-anchored sprite (apple) is projected and blended into the rendered image; reward is given when enough red pixels are visible.
Sim-to-real regularization: random noise added to camera pose during training.

setting.backbone: PPO policy network (trained from scratch via RL; the simulator uses Gaussian Splatting splatfacto)
setting.training_data: RL in simulator built from a single phone video of a garden scene; PPO for 30,000 steps (Exp I), about 1M steps (Exp II)
setting.action_space: discrete: fixed-step x/y moves and z rotation (6 actions); Exp II: forward/back along heading plus rotation
setting.privileged: none at test time (policy sees only ego image); reconstruction of the scene from video is used for training

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark; only a custom sim-to-real action-match rate (Table sim_to_real: total 0.612 without regularization vs 0.783 with, over 1568 frames from 6 real clips). Other results are in figures.
results: Splatfacto is 45% faster to train and 291x faster at inference than nerfacto (17 vs 31 ms/iter; 7.8 vs 2270 ms/frame). PPO policies learn to find the goal in the garden scene, running at over 100 Hz. The sim-trained policy matches human-labelled optimal actions on 78.3% of 1568 real frames with regularization, versus 61.2% without.
limitations: Single garden scene; the real-world evaluation is offline action agreement with human labels, not closed-loop robot navigation, and there are no standard benchmarks or baselines.

Pipeline is manual and awkward: point clouds come from a separate NeRF model, are cropped by hand, and the policy fails where the goal is occluded; the Exp II policy did not fully converge after 1M steps.
No robot embodiment or dynamics, and no interaction with scene objects.
